stories.body: French authorities imposed overnight, area-specific curfews in parts of Paris and several northern cities after protests involving more than 500,000 people nationwide turned violent. Officials say public buildings were attacked and about 2,000 shops were looted. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said a nationwide state of emergency remains possible but that targeted curfews are more appropriate for now, while Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez acknowledged police had lost control in some places and offered his resignation, which President Emmanuel Macron refused.
stories.headline: France imposes partial curfews after violent weekend protests and looting

stories.body: President Volodymyr Zelensky accused the United States of holding up Patriot interceptor missiles paid for by European allies, deepening a dispute over military assistance and intelligence sharing. A Ukrainian presidential adviser told the BBC that incomplete or late US ballistic-missile warnings had already cost lives, although other intelligence flows continue. The White House said it had not changed intelligence sharing, but Kyiv also says restrictions on Starlink and Starshield have limited drone operations and may be intended to pressure Ukraine into concessions in negotiations with Russia.
stories.headline: Zelensky says US is delaying Patriot deliveries and providing unreliable missile warnings

stories.body: Japan has launched its Mars Moons Exploration mission, which will study Deimos and attempt to land on Phobos, collect at least 10 grams of material and return it to Earth in 2031. The spacecraft is expected to reach Phobos in August 2027, deploying a small rover before its own landing and sampling attempt. Scientists hope the samples will settle whether Mars’s moons formed from debris after a giant impact or were captured asteroids, and may also provide clues about the early solar system.
stories.headline: Japan launches five-year mission to return samples from Mars’s moon Phobos

stories.body: At least 53 people were killed and more than 200 wounded when three Houthi ballistic missiles struck the al-Alam training camp in Shabwa province, Yemen’s authorities said. The camp was training recruits for internal security forces, although the Houthis said they had targeted Saudi-backed enemy forces and officers. The strike is among the deadliest since Yemen’s civil war escalated again in September, as pro-government forces backed by a Saudi-led coalition fight the Iran-aligned Houthis across several fronts.
stories.headline: Houthi missile strike kills at least 53 security recruits in Yemen

stories.body: Drone attacks across Sudan have killed more than 160 people in recent days, according to medics and rights groups, with both the Sudanese army and the Rapid Support Forces accused of strikes. The deadliest reported attack hit a transport hub near a market in al-Dibab, West Kordofan, killing 80 people as villagers gathered to travel home. The UN condemned the attacks, which are increasingly hitting civilians and essential services in a war that has displaced about 13 million people since 2023.
stories.headline: Escalating drone attacks kill at least 160 people across Sudan

stories.body: China’s economy grew 4.5% year on year in the third quarter, above forecasts and up from 4.3% in the previous quarter, putting it on course to meet Beijing’s 4.5% to 5% annual target. Manufacturing output rose 6% in September, supported by exports of electronics, AI-related equipment and vehicles. But domestic demand remains weak: retail sales rose only 1.1%, while investment fell sharply and property investment dropped 20.6% in the first nine months of the year.
stories.headline: China’s economy outpaces forecasts as AI-related exports rise

stories.body: Major Democratic and Republican Senate super PACs paused broadcast advertising in Georgia as public polling and fundraising point to a strong re-election position for Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff over Republican Representative Mike Collins. Senate Majority PAC and the Republican Senate Leadership Fund still hold future reservations but can redirect the money, with the latter spending far less than its initially announced $44 million investment. Republicans are shifting resources toward more competitive races, although they continue to watch Georgia’s governor’s contest closely.
stories.headline: Outside groups pull back Georgia advertising as Jon Ossoff opens a wide Senate-race lead

stories.body: The US Supreme Court will consider whether parents challenging admissions policies at four selective Maryland middle schools have enough evidence to pursue claims of intentional discrimination against Asian-American students. The Montgomery County district’s policy screens all pupils for academic potential and uses a lottery, while comparing results among students of similar family income. Lower courts found no evidence of discriminatory intent and noted that Asian-American students were not underrepresented among those admitted, but a ruling for the parents could revive the lawsuit.
stories.headline: Supreme Court agrees to hear school-admissions case involving race

stories.body: Storm Adam brought torrential rain and severe flooding to eastern Spain, with Oliva in Valencia province recording more than 450 litres per square metre in 24 hours. Four deaths have been reported, including two people in Oliva, while emergency services and military units used helicopters to rescue residents trapped in homes or on rooftops. Authorities confined residents in 145 municipalities in Valencia and Alicante at the height of the emergency, though the storm was beginning to ease and restrictions were being lifted in some places.
stories.headline: Storm Adam floods eastern Spain, killing four and prompting mass rescues

stories.body: Supreme Court judge Pablo Llarena upheld his decision to lift Spain’s domestic arrest warrants for former Catalan president Carles Puigdemont and former ministers Toni Comín and Lluís Puig. He applied Constitutional Court doctrine on the amnesty law’s treatment of alleged misuse of public funds, despite criticising that court’s interpretation. The decision means Puigdemont can return to Spain without being detained, but it does not end the criminal proceedings or formally grant amnesty; those decisions remain for the Supreme Court’s criminal chamber.
stories.headline: Supreme Court confirms lifting of Puigdemont’s arrest warrant under amnesty doctrine

stories.body: Spain marked 15 years since ETA announced the definitive end of its armed campaign on 20 October 2011. The Basque separatist group, which killed more than 850 people over roughly five decades, later dissolved in 2018 after sustained police, political and social pressure. Reporting on the anniversary notes that victims’ memory and the meaning of ETA’s defeat remain politically contested, despite the broad relief that followed the end of violence.
stories.headline: Spain marks 15 years since ETA ended its armed campaign amid continuing political divisions

stories.body: Spain’s government is preparing a decree that would require data centres to cover 80% of their electricity consumption with renewable energy and account for that use hour by hour. The proposal responds to the large energy and water demands of data-centre cooling and AI computing. The industry says the requirements would make projects economically unviable and amount to a de facto moratorium, warning that investment could shift to Portugal or Italy; the draft is now before the Council of State.
stories.headline: Spain plans rules to reduce data centres’ environmental impact

stories.body: Heavy rain has led Rodalies to impose speed restrictions, causing average delays of more than 20 minutes on the R1, R2 Sud, R11 and southern regional services. Barcelona’s L3 metro line returned to normal after water accumulated at Liceu station, while authorities continued to monitor road and rail disruption caused by the adverse weather. Passengers on an early R4 service also had to change trains at Cornellà de Llobregat after its windscreen wiper failed.
stories.headline: Flood-related speed restrictions disrupt Rodalies services across Catalunya

stories.body: Catalonia’s health department is investigating three further cases involving infants allegedly abused by their parents where medical staff may not have detected warning signs in time or where child-protection procedures may have failed. One concerns a three-month-old who died in June after previously visiting primary-care centres in Sabadell; the parents remain in custody. The inquiries follow an earlier case in which an infant’s severe injuries were not identified as suspected abuse after visits to several hospitals and a health centre.
stories.headline: Catalan health authorities investigate three more suspected child-abuse cases missed by the health system

stories.body: Mossos d’Esquadra officers charged at protesters during a demonstration against far-right agitator Vito Quiles’s planned appearance at the Autonomous University of Barcelona. The university had refused permission for his event, and police prevented him from entering campus, but more than a thousand demonstrators gathered and some threw fruit, paint balls and other objects at officers. Quiles later said he had gone to the Ikea area in Sabadell, where further confrontations were reported.
stories.headline: Mossos charge during UAB protest against far-right agitator Vito Quiles

stories.body: Castelldefels has suspended new licences for hotels and other tourist accommodation for up to a year while it examines whether some areas are saturated. The measure covers hotels, tourist apartments, holiday lets, campsites and other new accommodation capacity, though licences already granted and applications already formally under way are exempt. The PP and Som local government says the pause responds to housing pressure and the high ratio of tourist beds to residents in some neighbourhoods, rather than opposition to tourism itself.
stories.headline: Castelldefels pauses new hotel licences for a year to assess tourism saturation
